It's October. Andrei video-calls Mara late in the evening. He has a problem: since the holiday in August, he and Lena have been writing to each other every day. But he's in Sibiu and she's in Berlin.
Mara, I need your advice. It's about Lena.

We write to each other every day. We talk on the phone every evening. But I don't know what this is. Is it a relationship? A long-distance relationship? One thousand two hundred kilometres! What should I do?
First you should talk to her honestly. Ask her what she thinks. Not on the phone, but in person.
Exactly. If I were you, I'd come to Berlin. You've got a week off in November, haven't you?
Yes, but flights are expensive. And what if she says no?
You could stay with me, then it's only the flight. And if she says no, at least you'll know. That's better than asking yourself every evening: what is this?
And what would you say to her? I mean, if you were me?
I wouldn't say much. I'd go to her bakery at four in the morning and help her shape pretzels. Like in the spring. She'll do the rest.
You're the best sister in the world. But I won't say that a second time.
I've recorded it. And, Andrei? Bring Dad's honey. Lena has already asked.

No umlaut! “sollte” looks exactly like the Präteritum (“was supposed to”). The context makes the difference: “Du solltest kommen” = you should come (advice).

“raten” changes its vowel: ich rate, du rätst, er rät. And it takes the DATIVE: “Ich rate dir.” The same goes for “empfehlen”: “Ich empfehle dir das Buch.”

It was a Sunday at the end of October, shortly after six in the morning. Kastanienallee was still dark and empty. Only at the bakery was the light on, as always. Mara knocked on Ludwig's door. He opened it in his dressing gown, with sleepy eyes and Fritz in his arms.
Mara? Has something happened? Is something on fire?
No. But you should get dressed quickly. Your uniform, if you've still got it. And your cap. We have an appointment at half past six.

Ludwig looked at her for a long time. Then, without a single question, he went into the bedroom. Ten minutes later he came back, in an old blue uniform jacket that was a little too wide at the shoulders, and a cap on which a small, faded badge of the Berlin transport company gleamed. He had shaved. He looked twenty years younger.

In front of the building Lena was waiting with a flask of coffee and a bag of warm rolls. All three of them walked to the stop, with Fritz in front. Ludwig didn't ask anything, but Mara saw that his hands were shaking. Not from the cold.

And then, at half past six on the dot, it appeared round the corner. Slowly, with a loud, old-fashioned clang that echoed down the whole quiet street. A yellow Tatra tram, with round headlights like friendly eyes. The sign at the front didn't say “M1” but, as in the old days, “46 Prenzlauer Berg”. At the driver's window sat Mr Wolff, in full uniform, smiling.
The tram stopped right in front of them. The doors opened with an old, familiar hiss. Mr Wolff stood up, came down the three steps and saluted.
Good morning, Master Brandt. Car 5218, line 46. Your car. I checked in the archive. You drove it from 1979 to 1992. It's waiting for you.

Ludwig said nothing. He stood on the pavement and looked at the yellow tram like an old friend he hadn't seen for thirty years. Then he said, very quietly: “Kurt? Kurt Wolff? The little apprentice who could never brake?” Mr Wolff laughed: “I can now. You taught me.”

Ludwig got on. He sat down in the driver's seat, slowly, carefully, because of his back. He put his hands on the levers. He looked ahead at the tracks gleaming in the first grey light of the morning. Mr Wolff stood beside him, his hand resting calmly on his shoulder. Mara, Lena and Fritz sat in the first row, right behind.
Ludwig rang the bell. Twice, briefly, the way drivers used to when they set off. Then he slowly pulled away, and the old tram started moving with a deep hum that Mara felt through her whole body.

They drove the whole route. Along Kastanienallee, past the bakery, where Emre stood in the doorway waving. Along Schönhauser Allee, where Ludwig stopped at every stop, even though nobody was waiting, because that's just how it's done. Past the Mauerpark, where the grey-bearded trader was just setting up his stall and waved his cap, as if he had known. Ludwig drove calmly and surely, with his gut, as he had always said, and told a story at every corner.

At the Eberswalder Straße stop stood an old woman with a shopping trolley. You could tell she'd been waiting for the first bus, and she looked at the yellow tram in surprise. Ludwig stopped, opened the doors and called: “Please, get on! Everyone rides for free today!” The woman got on, sat down, and after two stops she said: “I know you. You're the driver with the guitar. You took me to work every morning in the eighties. You were always whistling.” Ludwig laughed out loud. “And you always had a red umbrella!” The woman nodded and suddenly looked very young. When she got off at Rosenthaler Platz, she said: “Thank you for the ride. The most beautiful one in thirty years.”

Here, at this stop, Ingrid waited for me for three days. Right here. Back then there was a greengrocer's there. She pretended to be buying apples. Three days in a row she bought apples. We had apple cake all winter.

Lena was laughing and crying at the same time. She had never heard this story. Mara took her hand. At the terminus, at Kupfergraben, right opposite Museum Island, Ludwig stopped the tram. The sun was just rising over the Spree, and the old water was glowing gold.

For a long time Ludwig sat motionless in the driver's seat. Then he took off his cap, turned round and looked at Mara. “You did this, didn't you?” he asked. Mara nodded. “You shouldn't have done that,” he said. “It was far too much work.” He paused. “Thank you, Mara. It was the most beautiful morning in many years.”

On the way back Mr Wolff drove. Ludwig sat in the first row next to Mara, with Fritz on his lap, and looked out of the window at his city. After a while he said: “You know, I heard you signed the contract. That you're staying.” Mara nodded again. “In your place,” said Ludwig, “I'd have done the same.” And then, after a pause, with a little smile: “But in my place I'm very glad about it.”
Fritz barked once, short and loud, as if he wanted to say that he thought so too. Then he fell asleep again, right on Ludwig's lap.
